Read every character and asset time act and every map, as saved, in the background. This can take minutes. The result is kept with the project for later sessions.
Stop the scan. The previous result, if any, is kept.

Type ID or name, e.g. 603 or Billboard
A number matches the action type exactly; text matches part of the action's name. Leave empty to match every action.
A field, property or list of the action, by name.
Part of a value's schema name. The action matches when it stores such a value (and, with a range, the value contains a number in it).
Only match values with a number between the two limits: a field's components, a constant, or any curve key's value.
The lowest and highest value to match, in the Action Inspector's display units.
Only actions that use this texture or model ID.
A texture or model ID (88610 for s88610). 0 matches any.
Only effects the project has changed: modified, added, unsaved, or with binder changes.
Search every effect in the background (loaded effects are searched in their current state).
Clear the inputs and the results.
Stop the search. Results found so far are kept.
Each matching action: its effect, node path, config and name, with the value that matched.
{0} found; the search stopped at {1}. Narrow the search to see the rest.
Which effects the list shows, in addition to the search.
Effects whose saved copy differs from the game's.
Effects the game doesn't have: created in the editor or added by the project.
Effects with edits or binder changes that haven't been saved.
Effects marked as favorites (kept with the project).
The effects selected most recently in this session, newest first.
Effects that draw with a texture or model whose ID starts with the typed number. The first use scans every effect.
Effects in which the last Project Check found problems.

Needs a scan of every effect.
Modified: differs from the game's copy
Added: the game has no such effect
Copy this effect, including unsaved edits, to a new ID in the binders you pick. The files are added on save.
A copy of {0} under a new ID. Saving adds it to each ticked binder (with a resource list, where the binder keeps one).
Duplicated {0} as {1} in {2} binder(s). It is written on save.

Pick which sfx binders hold this effect. An effect only plays from a binder the game has loaded, so add it to the binders of the character, map or object that uses it. Files are added or removed on save.
The binders that hold {0}. Tick a binder to add the effect to it; untick it to remove the effect. Nothing changes until you save.
The binders that hold the {0} picked effects. A ticked binder gets all of them, and an unticked one gets none. A binder marked with a count keeps each effect as it is until you click it.
An effect must stay in at least one binder. To remove it everywhere, use Delete Effect.
{0} was left in its binders: an effect must stay in at least one.
Remove the effect from every binder on save. Undo restores it, before or after the save.
Delete {0} effect(s)? Their files are removed from every binder on save. Anything still using them is listed below and will refer to an effect that no longer exists.
Deleted {0} effect(s). Their files are removed on save.
Move this effect to a new ID in the same binders and, optionally, point every effect that starts it at the new ID.
{0} moves to the new ID in its {1} binder(s). On save, the old file is removed and the new one added.
Point the {0} effect(s) that start it at the new ID
{0} param field(s) hold the old ID and are not changed. Click one to open it:
Aliases are kept by ID, so the old ID's alias stays with the old ID.
Moved {0} to {1}. Updated {2} call(s) in other effects.
Replace the effect's content with the game's copy. This is a normal edit: undo it, or save to keep it. Binder changes are not reverted.
The effect matches the game's copy and has no unsaved edits.
Reverted {0} effect(s) to the game's copy.
List every value that differs from the game's copy of this effect.
List every value that differs between this effect and another.
List every value that differs between the two picked effects.

Nodes are matched by their position in the tree, as the game references them, so a node added early shows as changes to the later nodes. Values show as integers, with a float reading where one is likely.
The effects that start this one through a Proxy node, and the param fields that hold its ID. Click one to go there. TAE events and map parts are not searched.
Read the params again. Param edits made since the last scan aren't seen until you do.
The effects this one starts through its Proxy nodes. Click one to go there.
Favorites are marked with a star and listed by the Favorites filter. They're kept with the project.
Name this effect. The name is saved to the project's Particles aliases immediately, so other editors show it in their effect fields.
The alias for {0}. Leave it empty to remove the project's alias.
Write the effect, including unsaved edits, as a {0} file to share or keep as a backup.
Read a {0} file into the project, either as a new effect in the binders you pick or over an existing effect's content.
The file is a {0} effect, but this project uses {1}. It may not read or play correctly.
{0} keeps its binders, and its content is replaced by the file's. Undo restores it.
Imported {0} as {1}. It is written on save.
Failed to read {0} as a {1} effect file.
The file is a {0} effect, but this project uses {1}, so it can't be used here.
This ID holds different effects in different binders (versions). Each version keeps its own binders, so you can't change the binders and ID of all versions at once.
Check every effect the project has changed (modified, added, unsaved or with binder changes) for structure problems, missing textures and models, and effects in no binder.
Click a problem to open the effect at that node. Textures are only reported when no sfx binder holds them, as an effect can use textures from another loaded binder.
{0} changed effect(s) checked: {1} problem(s) in {2} effect(s).
Uses {0}, which no sfx binder holds.
The effect is in no binder.
Failed to read the favorite effects from {0}.
Failed to save the favorite effects to {0}.
Effect tables in {0}: {1} record(s) added, {2} removed.
Couldn't read the effect table {0} in {1}. It was left unchanged.
The effect's states and node tree. Each node runs the config its state chooses, and each config lists the states that use it.
Show or hide this node and everything under it in playback. Alt+click to show only this node's branch. A hidden node still runs, and visibility isn't saved to the file.
Show only this node's branch in playback and hide every other branch. Alt+clicking an eye does the same.
Hide every branch of the root in playback. Showing a branch again shows all of it.
Add a copy of the selected node, with its configs, actions and child nodes, just after it.
Remove the selected node and everything under it. The root node can't be removed.
Copy the node and everything under it, to paste into this effect or another effect of the same game.
Copy the node and everything under it, then remove it.
Paste the copied node (from {0}) just after this node, as its sibling.
Paste the copied node (from {0}) as this node's last child.
The copy came from {0}. Each game lays out actions differently, so it can't be pasted here.
[FX Editor] Pasted from {0}. It had {1} states and this effect has {2}, so {3} state config map(s) were adjusted. Check which config each state uses.
Under a Levels of Detail node, the order is the detail order: the first child is the closest level.
Add a saved template as this node's last child.
No templates are saved for this game yet.
Move a template file to the .archive folder inside the templates folder.

Save the node and everything under it as a template for this project, in:
{0}
A template with this name already exists and will be replaced.
Fit the viewport to this node's current particles (or the whole effect, if the node draws none). Needs Highlight Selected on.
Write a note for this node. Notes are kept with the project, not in the effect file.
Leave empty to remove the note. On an effect with unsaved changes, the note is written when the effect is saved.
Select the effect this Proxy node starts.
Add a copy of this config after the node's other configs. No state uses it until you assign one with Use for State.
Remove this config. States that used it switch to the first config. A node's only config can't be removed.
Make a state run this config.
This node has no state config map, so it always uses its first config.
Copy this action's values, to paste over another action of the same kind.
Replace this action with the copied one (from {0}): its type and all its values.
The copied action can only replace an action of the same kind ({0}).
Replace this Proxy node with copies of the nodes of the effect it starts, so you can edit them here. Asks first, and lists anything that would play differently.
This Proxy node is under a Node Emitter, which picks among its children, so its target's nodes can't move into it.
This Proxy node is under a Levels of Detail node, where each child is one level, so its target's nodes can't move into it.
Replace this Proxy node with copies of the {1} node(s) of {0}? {0} itself is not changed.
It should play the same: the effect has one state, ends the same way and has the same effect settings.
The started effect has more than one state. In every state here, the copied nodes run the config they use in its state 0, and its own state changes are lost.
The started effect's state 0 conditions differ from this effect's (e.g. it ends after its own time). They are lost: the copied nodes end when this effect does.
The started effect's root settings (termination mode, view distance, initial simulation time) differ from this effect's. The copied nodes use this effect's settings.
This effect has several states and the node isn't directly under the root. The new effect's state time starts when the Proxy node first runs, so its state changes may happen later than this effect's.
Move this node and everything under it into a new effect, started from here by a Proxy node. On save, the new effect is added to every binder that holds this one.
The {0} node and its branch move into a new effect, with this effect's states and root settings. A Proxy node that starts it replaces the node.
An effect with this ID already exists.
It will be added to the {0} binder(s) that hold this effect: {1}. Its ffxreslist starts as a copy of this effect's.
[FX Editor] Extracted {0} from {1}. It is written to {2} binder(s) on the next save.

Create a starter template of each kind (each appearance type, Node Emitter, Levels of Detail) from the simplest example in this project's effects. They are saved as "Starter - ..." templates; building again replaces them.
[FX Editor] The starter templates couldn't be built.
Show this state's configs in the viewport's debug shapes and the node summaries. Playback still starts in state 0 and follows the conditions.
Add a state with no conditions at the end. Every node uses its first state's config in it until you change it.
Insert a copy of this state just after it, with its conditions and the config each node uses in it. Later states, and the conditions that move to them, are renumbered.
Remove this state. Conditions that moved to it end the effect instead, and later states are renumbered. Asks first.
An effect needs at least one state.
{0} condition(s) move to state {1}. They will end the effect instead.
States {0} and later move down by one. The conditions and node configs that refer to them are updated.
This is the start state. The effect will start in what is now state 1.
Swap this state with the one above or below. Conditions and node configs move with the states. The effect starts in state 0.
A state sets which config each node runs. Its conditions decide when the effect moves to another state or ends.
The effect starts in this state.
{0} node(s) run a different config in this state than in state 0.
Where the effect goes when the condition is true: another state (whose state time restarts) or the end, where each node follows its Termination action.
The external value ID the game sets (0 = Terminate, 1 = precipitation, 2 = time of day, ...). Set preview values in the Tools window.
Add a condition at the end: end the effect after 1 second in this state. Conditions are checked in order, and the first one that is true is taken.
Seconds since the effect entered this state.
A value the game sets, by ID.
Thought to depend on movement. The preview reads it as 0.
This Proxy node starts the effect it is in.
This Proxy node starts {0}, which isn't in any loaded binder.
This Proxy node has no effect ID.
This node has no configs, so it does nothing.
The state config map points past the node's {0} configs.
The state config map has {0} entries, but the effect has {1} states.

[FX Editor] The node notes couldn't be written to {0}.
The selected item. Values are shown in display units (seconds, degrees); the raw view shows what the file stores.
Select an action in the Effect Tree to see its values.
When a condition is true, the effect moves to its target state or ends.
The action's name, type and slot, from the FXR schema.
Show the words and properties exactly as the file stores them.
Show values whose purpose isn't known yet (named unk_ in the schema).
The FXR schema has no layout for this action in {0}, so only its raw values are shown.
This action stores more values than the schema describes, so only its raw values are shown.
Greyed-out names aren't stored in the file and use the schema default. Editing one adds it to the file.
Values whose purpose isn't known yet.
Shown in display units (e.g. seconds or degrees). The file stores a different unit.
Not stored in the file. The schema default is shown.
Go to {0} in the FX Editor
Open the FX Editor with this effect selected. Ctrl+clicking the value does the same.
{0}: no sfx binder holds this effect
An ID (88300) or a file name (s88300, s88300_a, s88300_a.tpf, s88300.flver). The file stores the ID, and the slot decides which texture type is loaded. 0 is none.
Not an ID or a resource name. It is discarded when you leave the field.
The action's fields as stored (index, hex, int, float) and its properties.
Play the selected effect in the viewport.

Draw Distortion particles (which bend the scene behind them with a normal map, stirred or twisted) and RadialBlur particles (blurred towards their centre). They read a copy of the scene taken before particles are drawn, so other particles behind them aren't bent.

Draw LensFlare layers: sprites at their source, or moved across the screen through its centre, drawn over the scene and faded by how much of the source is visible. DS3's LightShaft is also drawn this way, as layered glows at its source. This is an approximation, as the action is barely documented.

Draw the GPU particle systems (GPUStandardParticle, GPUSparkParticle and their Correct versions), simulated here on the CPU as billboards (stretched along their motion when traced) and sparks. The preview keeps at most 4000 particles per system; the game keeps many more.
Draw PointSprite, BillboardEx and MultiTextureBillboardEx particles as textured quads with their blend modes. A texture that is still loading, or that no binder holds, draws as a soft round spot.
Scale the colour of every billboard. Effect colours are over-bright (HDR) values, and exactly how the game maps them to the screen isn't known, so use this to match the game's look.
The brightness multiplier. 1x draws the colours as stored.
{0} trail and line segments, {1} models, {2} of {3} lights.

In the game, an effect usually moves: it flies with a projectile or swings with a weapon. Trails, equal-distance emitters and detached particles depend on that motion, so the preview can move the effect the same way.
Still: the effect stays at the origin. Forward: it flies along +Z, like a projectile. Swing: it moves around a circle, like a weapon tip in a slash. Changing this replays the effect.
How fast the effect flies forward.
The radius of the circle the effect moves around, about the Y axis.
How fast the effect moves around the circle.
Fit a newly selected effect into view. Turn off to keep the camera in place when switching effects (Frame still works on request).

Show a value in the preview while you type, drag or pick it (in the Action Inspector and the Curve Editor), not only once it's committed. The preview keeps its playback time. Each change is still one undo step.

Wind, gravity and turbulence volumes push the nodes and particles that have a force movement action (NodeForceSpeed/Acceleration, ParticleForceSpeed/Acceleration). Most of those effects have no force of their own: in game, weather wind or another effect's wind moves them, and the preview wind stands in for that.
Let the effect's own WindForce, GravityForce, TurbulenceForce and CancelForce volumes act on it.
A steady wind everywhere, standing in for weather wind, to show how force-driven effects drift.
The wind direction around the vertical axis (0° is +Z, the direction of Forward motion).
The wind's force. Vanilla wind volumes range from about 2 to 50 (force × its random multiplier).
Move the camera with the effect, so it stays in view. The wireframes stay where the effect started.

Scale the intensity of the effect's lights. Light intensities vary a lot between games (around 0.1 in DS3, around 50 in AC6), and how they map to the viewport's lights isn't known, so use this to match the game.
The light intensity multiplier. 1x uses diffuseMultiplier × the colour's alpha as stored.
Draw Model and RichModel particles with their FLVER (sfx model s<id>), lit like other models. Their colour, UV scrolling and animation aren't applied yet. At most 200 per appearance.
Add PointLight and SpotLight particles to the viewport as lights, which light the models in the viewport. The viewport draws at most 15, the brightest ones.
Mark each light with a cross and a ring at its range, and each spot light with its direction.
No binder holds these textures, so they draw as soft spots: {0} ({1} in all).
The running effect: its current state, and how many particles and nodes it has. Its own conditions change its state, based on the time and the external values below.
Select an effect to run it.
Terminated: emitters have stopped, and the remaining particles play out.
Finished: nothing of the effect remains. Restart to play it again.
The preview reached its limit of {0} particles or {1} nodes, so some weren't created.
A Proxy node starts an effect that isn't in the project, so it shows nothing.
End the effect, as reaching state -1 does: each node then follows its Termination action. Restarting, scrubbing back or editing plays it again from the start without this.
Draw each live particle as a small white cross on top of its billboard, to show particles that are too small, too faint or hidden. At most 20000 are drawn.
Start, pause and restart the effect's clock, and frame the effect in the viewport.
Start or pause the effect's clock.
Move the camera so the whole effect is in view.
The effect's time since it started, in seconds.
Drag to move to a time. This pauses playback.
How long the effect plays before it loops or stops. Effects have no stored length (their state conditions end them), so set this by hand.
Restart the effect when the playback length is reached. Otherwise, playback stops there.
How fast the effect's clock runs compared with real time.
The playback speed. 1x is real time.
The effect state the wireframes show. Each node uses the config its StateConfigMap gives this state.
The state index, from 0 to the effect's last state.
Values the game sets on a running effect. State conditions and some properties read them; for example, Terminate (0) ends an effect. IDs not listed read as 0.
The value the effect reads for this ID.
Remove this value. It then reads as 0.
The ID of an external value to add.
Add the external value with this ID.
What the viewport draws for the selected effect.
Draw each emitter's shape (point, disk, rectangle, sphere, box or cylinder) at its node, with an orange arrow for the particles' initial direction, if it has one.
Draw each node's origin as short red (X), green (Y) and blue (Z) lines. Proxy nodes are marked with a magenta cross.
Click to edit this curve in the Curve Editor.
The property picked in the Action Inspector: how its value changes over time, its keys and its modifiers. Each change is one undo step, made when you release a value or a dragged key.
Click a property's name in the Action Inspector to edit it here.
The selected value isn't a property of this action.
The action and property being edited, and what drives it.
the node's active time when the particle was emitted
nothing: the value at time 0 is used
How the value is stored: a constant, or keys joined in steps, straight lines or curves.
Changing the function keeps the keys where possible. Tangents reset to flat when changing between Bezier and Hermite, as they mean different things.
Each key's value holds until the next key.
Smooth curves between the keys, shaped by each key's slopes.
Eased curves between the keys, shaped by two angles stored on the key before each segment. The graph approximates the game's curve.
A Hermite curve per component, each with its own keys (AC6 and Nightreign).
Repeat the curve after its last key. A looping curve with all its keys at 0 has no length, which the game reads as invalid.
The length a Component Hermite curve stores. It grows to cover the last key.
The value over time, in the inspector's units. Shaded bands show the range the random modifiers spread it across.
Drag a key to move it in time and value; yellow keys belong to the selected component. Double-click to add a key. Scroll to zoom, and right-drag to pan.
The keys in time order. Keys are re-sorted when an edit is committed.
The constant value. To convert it to keys, change the Function above.
Component Hermite keeps keys per component. Pick which component's keys are listed and dragged.
The key's time, in seconds of whatever drives the property.
The key's value, one per component.
The slope as the curve leaves this key, in value per second.
The slope as the curve arrives at this key, in value per second.
The tangent angles of the segment after this key, in radians as stored (0 to about 1.57). Unlike the values, they aren't converted.
Remove this key. A curve keeps at least one key.
Add a key after the last one, with the curve's value there.
Changes applied to the property's value: random variation per instance, or scaling by an external value. Ranges are shown in the inspector's units.
Add a modifier. It starts with no effect: a range of 0 or a factor of 1.
A random value between the base minus the delta and the base plus the delta, per particle or node.
Add a random value between the minimum and the maximum, per particle or node.
A random value within the fraction of the base value (0.5: between half and one and a half times it).
Multiply the value by a factor that depends on an external value the game sets, such as the time of day.
Like External Value 1, but read only when the effect starts (Elden Ring uses it for blood visibility, AC6 for external value 2000).
One value per component, in the inspector's units (fractions aren't converted).
The seed used to pick the random value, per component. Particles with the same seeds vary together.
The ID of the external value that sets the factor (0 Terminate, 1 precipitation, 2 time of day, ...).
A key of the factor curve: the external value, then the factor for each component.
Loading effects: {0} of {1} ready. Playback waits until they load.
Loading effects: {0} of {1} ready. Each starts once it loads.
The Project Check reads FXR3 effects, so it isn't available for this game's effects.
The binders hold {0} different effects with this ID. Pick the version to edit in the Effect Tree. Each version is saved only to its own binders.
The binders hold different effects with this ID (Demon's Souls: ds_sfxbnd_main versus the others). Each version is edited separately and saved only to the binders listed with it.
The state the effect moves to when this exit's condition is true.
How the two values below are compared. Only the operator changes; the values stay the same.
Whether both conditions below must be true (&&) or either one (||).
A value passed to the effect (by argument index), read by one of two evaluators whose difference is unknown. The second number is an unknown int stored with it (1 or 3 in vanilla).

The resources the effect lists as needed, as written by the game's build tool (vanilla lists often hold more than is used). Saving keeps them and adds any IDs an edit introduces, such as a new texture ID.
{0}: added {1} new ID(s) to its resource lists.
The value's stored type sets the interpolation and looping. Only the keys can be edited.
This effect is made of several complete effects with the same ID (Demon's Souls). Pick the one to show.
A state runs its own actions. Its exits decide when the effect moves to another state or ends.
No exits: the effect stays in this state.
The called action or effect. Click to select it in the Effect Tree.
A value stored with a factor next to it.

Part of a packed condition (Dark Souls node types 136 to 140). The node type sets its operator and constants, which can't be changed. You can edit the arguments under it; in the distance conditions (138 to 140), the second argument number is always 1.

You can edit and save values, exits and the parts inside an effect (states, actions, calls). Use the Effect List to duplicate, delete, renumber, move between binders, revert, compare, export and import whole effects.
Add an empty state at the end, with no actions and no exits. Once the effect reaches it, it stays there.
Insert a copy of this state, with its actions and exits, just after it. Later states, and the exits that lead to them, are renumbered.
Remove this state. Exits that lead to it end the effect instead, and later states are renumbered. Asks first.
{0} exit(s) lead to state {1}. They will end the effect instead.
States {0} to {1} move down by one. The exits that lead to them are updated.
Swap this state with the one above or below. Exits move with the states. The effect starts in state 0.
Add an action to the end of this state. Each action starts as its most common version in this project's effects. The list is built the first time it opens, which reads every effect once.
No effects could be read to take actions from.
Insert a copy of this exit, with the same target and condition, just after it.
Remove this exit from the state.
Insert a copy of this action, with all its values and calls, just after it.
Remove this action from its state.
Insert a copy of this call, with its values, just after it in its list.
Remove this call from its list. A list keeps at least one call.
This call fills one of its action's fixed slots, so it can't be copied, removed or moved. Only lists made of calls can change length.
Move this item up or down one place in its list. The order of a state's actions and of a list's calls can change how the effect plays.
Add an exit that ends the effect, with this project's most common exit condition. Change its target and values in the Inspector.
Copy this action or call, with its values and calls, to paste into another state or list of this game.
Insert a copy of the copied item (from {0}). An action goes into a state's actions, and a call into a list of calls.
Nothing of this kind has been copied. Copy a state action to paste an action, or a call to paste a call.
The copied item comes from {0}. It can only be pasted into effects of the same game.
This slot has only one type in this game's effects.

Switch this slot between the value types the game's own effects use for it, keeping its value. A constant becomes a curve with one key at 0, a curve becomes a constant of its first key, and curves keep their keys.
